b: I see a little treasure in a white shirt and blue shorts, with no dreams or expectations at all. There's no excitement on his face. Today he is going to meet the first disappointment of his life. That child is unlikely to know that soon he will be crying for the mother who leaves him at school. I watch that little boy, knowing nothing of this, trying in baby talk to find the answers to all the secrets of life

His look is nothing new to me. I see the road I have travelled before my eyes. Oiled hair parted in the middle. Holy ash smeared on the forehead without measure. It competes with the leftover powder on both cheeks. A school bag on his back. To balance its weight, a water bottle hanging from his neck in front

When I see that boy, a wish peeps out from the depths of my mind. In a society where even a stranger's affection for a little child has become poison, I can't satisfy my wish by talking to him. I glance at him from the corner of my eye. As the left shoulder strap of his school bag, which was hiding it, shifts a little, I too see the sight that Thirunalaippovar saw at Thillai. The Lord of all, who emerged from hiding in the form of the lingam, is the witness there. It shows that my bond with that boy is greater than many ties of the umbilical cord. That is the bond called Hindu College

I don't want to begin with "in our day" and all that. I'm not that old. I am still a six-year-old child in a much older body. The boy who walked holding my first-year teacher's hand is still hiding inside me. When I think of my school, I turn into him. The sights open up for me through his eyes
To a three-foot child, everything looks enormous. I too think back as that boy. The decorated arch that stands welcoming at the entrance rises up before my eyes.

As soon as you enter, on the left, facing east, Pillaiyar in a small shrine. The scent of perfumes and flowers is a little stronger there alone. Beside him, Vani with her veena, seated on a white lotus. She has seen many changes over time. At her feet, four great sons who speak poetry in the Tamil that lived at Keezhadi. It seems they stand there as if to say, by their very sight, that they are the pillars guarding our mother, the college.

Right, left, straight ahead: buildings all around. That six-year-old didn't know what any of them were. But he understood that the building straight ahead had some special greatness. You could call it the sanctum of a temple. You could call it the finial on the temple tower. There, a man whom no colour but white ever touched has stayed in my memory. A weapon in his hand. Perhaps because God has a weapon. Taking his ringing voice for the sound of the temple bell, the boy goes in

Walking a little further on those small legs, the grandeur opens up even more. All around, the wall-towers man has raised. In the middle, a good piece of land left as a concession to Mother Nature; on that good land, a spreading lawn. In between, water standing from yesterday's rain; a white egret that has come from somewhere to drink it. Though it is fenced and guarded all round, many trees grown as high as the sky stand as extra guards. As their king, that banyan tree on the right. Today, having sent the memories of time down through its roots into the earth, it has given up its earthly body and stands in my heart in a body of glory.

If you ask whether all this is my mother, no! This is just ANATOMY! Like the nails, flesh and blood of a body. What breathes life into all of it are thousands of hearts. Students, teachers, staff: all of them are the living cells of my mother. Though the cells renew themselves as time changes, unlike the human body my college never grows old. Like a living river that never runs dry, she reigns on even after 70 years.

Not all my school memories are fixed like a nail in green wood. Forgetting is human nature, after all. Some are forgotten. But not all of them have vanished. I guard those treasures, which rise up as memory recalls them one after another, so that they don't go missing in the chest of time. The prefects in their "ties", standing at intervals in the early morning; the rest of the students like lines of ants following the way they showed. Though we did it resentfully back then, today whenever I see people who don't know how to stand in a queue, this scene comes back to me

The Panchapuranam sung every morning. After it, the principal's words of advice. At the end, the students eagerly waiting for the lesson that would disappear into the time for meeting teachers. The college anthem, which the mouth murmurs by itself without needing the brain, at the sound coming on the wind. Last, the national anthem we heard in Tamil. These became habits in memory, like a daily puja.

Many of the teachers who were there when I studied are no longer at the school. To share my memories of them would take many years; a thousand memories. The memories of them I would like to record as a crowning touch won't taste of anything to others. Because not only pain, but pleasure too, is known only in one's own experience. But even today, though I don't know it by heart, the teachers' song I heard them sing echoes many times in every corner of my mind.

I'm not going to lie and say I was someone who played and enjoyed himself in the twenty-minute interval. I admit, truthfully, that I wasn't. Even so, I record it as a witness to the sights my eyes saw. I have seen the miracle of a plastic bottle turning into a football in a break not even long enough to eat. The white uniforms heading for the pavilion by the gate on the Ramanathan College side would all come back in the afternoon soaked in a brown spray of rain. When the back pages of an exercise book meet Sellotape, a cricket ball is ready. You understand at that moment the secret of why the planks of the back desks keep splitting. Perhaps it was for fear of that paper ball, which flew more than a mile, that the teachers too filled the staff room during the interval.

There is still so much to tell. Lessons learned in the shade of the banyan tree; floods in the Aippasi rain that drowned us to the knees; the diamond jubilee of the 60th year: I have a thousand stories to string together in order. But all of them can only be enjoyed through experience. However much colour you paint on with words, their meaning dissolves in the flow of time. So I leave them as pictures in the memories of those who saw them.

We are children of one mother. We say our clan is one. My college made us feel this. In English they say 13 is an unlucky number. For me, those 13 years were the time that heaped luck on me. I don't remember the day I first set foot in my school. Nor do I remember the day I finally stepped out and left. But if today I am trying a little to reach some height in life, the ladder for it still stands, to this day, in her heart.

They say even a crow thinks its own chick is a golden chick. To my mother the college, I may not be a golden chick. But to me she is no crow; she is the gem of the black cobra. I don't agree to say, if there is another birth, let me be your son again. This one birth, crawling at her feet, is enough. I have received the fruit of a thousand penances.
note: Thirunalaippovar (the saint Nandanar), barred from entering the Chidambaram (Thillai) temple because of his caste, was granted his vision of Shiva when the great Nandi statue moved aside; here, the shifting bag strap reveals the school crest. Vani is Saraswati, goddess of learning, who holds a veena. Keezhadi is an excavated ancient Tamil city. The Panchapuranam is a set of five Shaiva hymns sung at morning worship. Aippasi is the rainy Tamil month of October–November. A cobra is said to carry a precious gem in its hood.
